steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: A questionnaire is a set of written questions used to collect data from respondents.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Open questions allow free-text answers (e.g. 'What do you think about…?'); they give detailed responses but are hard to analyse.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Closed questions give a fixed set of response options (e.g. tick boxes, Likert scales); they are easy to analyse but limit answers.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Leading questions influence the respondent to answer in a particular way — they must be avoided.

steps.title: Try it yourself
steps.body: Q: What is the difference between an open and a closed question? | Q: Why should leading questions be avoided? | Q: What is a double-barrelled question?

steps.title: Check your answers
steps.body: An open question allows free-text answers giving detailed responses; a closed question offers fixed options that are easy to analyse but limit responses. | Because they bias the results by encouraging a particular answer, making the data unrepresentative of respondents' true views. | A question that asks two things at once, making it unclear which part the respondent is answering, e.g. 'Do you enjoy maths and science?'

steps.title: Exam tips
steps.body: When criticising a question, use the correct term: 'leading', 'double-barrelled', 'overlapping options', 'ambiguous'. Always suggest an improved version of a flawed question, not just what is wrong. Closed question response boxes must be non-overlapping and cover all likely answers — add 'Other' if needed. Pilot study questions are very common — remember to say it is a small-scale trial run. If asked about response rate, mention both how to maximise it and the problem of non-response bias.
